cls: Antiarrhythmic - non-selective beta-blocker with class III (potassium-channel-blocking) activity
pharm: A beta-adrenergic blocker that also prolongs cardiac repolarisation (class III action), used for ventricular and atrial arrhythmias
quick: Start 80 mg twice daily, titrate (usual 80-160 mg BID; max ~320 mg/day) - in-hospital initiation with ECG/QT and CrCl
Take on an empty stomach; food (esp. antacids) reduces absorption
Crosses placenta; use only if benefit outweighs risk; monitor neonate
Excreted in milk in high amounts; avoid/monitor infant
ECG/QTc, heart rate, electrolytes (K/Mg), CrCl, blood pressure
summary: Sotalol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker that also has class III antiarrhythmic activity, prolonging the cardiac action potential and QT interval by blocking potassium channels. It is used to treat documented life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and to maintain sinus rhythm in symptomatic atrial fibrillation/flutter (the AF formulation, e.g. Betapace AF/Sotylize, is dosed for that purpose). It carries a BOXED WARNING for proarrhythmia, including torsades de pointes, with the risk dependent on dose, QT prolongation, renal function and electrolytes; therefore therapy must be INITIATED (and re-initiated, and uptitrated) in a facility with continuous ECG and QT monitoring and resuscitation available, generally for a minimum of 3 days. Dosing is by creatinine clearance because sotalol is eliminated renally and largely unchanged. The usual oral start is 80 mg twice daily, titrated to effect (commonly 80-160 mg twice daily, maximum about 320 mg/day for ventricular arrhythmia). Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia and avoid other QT-prolonging drugs.
indications: Documented life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias (e.g. sustained ventricular tachycardia)
Maintenance of normal sinus rhythm in patients with symptomatic atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter (AF-specific products)

dosage.d: 80 mg twice daily initially; titrate gradually (usually after >=3 days) to 80-160 mg twice daily; maximum about 320 mg/day (640 mg/day only in refractory life-threatening cases)
dosage.t: Orally twice daily, on an empty stomach
dosage.n: Initiate in hospital with continuous ECG/QT monitoring; correct K+/Mg2+ first

dosage.d: 80 mg twice daily initially; may increase to 120 mg twice daily; dose interval extended by CrCl
dosage.n: Initiate/uptitrate with ECG/QT monitoring; do not start if baseline QTc >450 ms

dosage.d: Ventricular: CrCl >60 mL/min give every 12 h; 30-60 mL/min every 24 h; 10-30 mL/min every 36-48 h; <10 individualise. AF product uses similar interval extension
dosage.t: Extend dosing interval as CrCl falls
dosage.n: Allow extra time to steady state before each up-titration

dosage.d: Do not initiate if baseline QTc >450 ms; reduce dose or discontinue if QTc prolongs to >=500 ms during therapy
dosage.t: Monitor QT 2-4 h after each dose during titration
dosage.n: Risk of torsades is dose- and QT-dependent

admin: INITIATE, re-initiate and up-titrate in a facility with continuous ECG monitoring, QT measurement and cardiac resuscitation, generally for at least 3 days
Calculate creatinine clearance and base the dosing interval on it; sotalol is eliminated renally and mostly unchanged
Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia before and during treatment; avoid concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
Take on an empty stomach; food (especially antacids/milk) reduces absorption
Do not start if baseline QTc exceeds 450 ms; monitor QT 2-4 hours after dosing and reduce/stop if QTc reaches >=500 ms
Do not stop abruptly in patients with ischaemic heart disease - taper to avoid rebound
moa: Sotalol is a racemic non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist (the l-isomer provides most of the beta-blockade) that, at therapeutic doses, also exerts class III antiarrhythmic activity by blocking the rapid component of the delayed-rectifier potassium current. Beta-blockade slows heart rate, reduces AV-nodal conduction and myocardial oxygen demand (class II effect), while potassium-channel blockade prolongs the action-potential duration, effective refractory period and QT interval in atrial and ventricular tissue (class III effect). These combined actions suppress re-entrant arrhythmias but also produce the dose-dependent QT prolongation that underlies its torsades-de-pointes risk.

absolute: Congenital or acquired long QT syndrome
Sinus bradycardia (<50 bpm), sick sinus syndrome, or second-/third-degree AV block without a functioning pacemaker
Bronchial asthma or related bronchospastic conditions
Severe renal failure with creatinine clearance below the threshold for the AF product, uncorrected hypokalaemia, and known hypersensitivity
relative: Recent myocardial infarction with reduced ejection fraction
monitor: ECG: QT/QTc interval and heart rate (2-4 h after dosing during titration)
Renal function (creatinine clearance) to guide dosing
Blood pressure and signs of heart failure

preg: Sotalol crosses the placenta and is found in amniotic fluid; it has been used to treat fetal/maternal arrhythmias but may cause neonatal beta-blockade (bradycardia, hypoglycaemia, hypotension). Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk, with fetal/neonatal monitoring.
lact: Sotalol is excreted into breast milk in concentrations higher than maternal plasma. If used during breastfeeding, monitor the infant for signs of beta-blockade (bradycardia, poor feeding); avoidance or careful monitoring is advised.
renal: Sotalol is eliminated by the kidneys largely unchanged, so the dosing interval must be extended according to creatinine clearance (e.g. for ventricular arrhythmia: every 12 h if CrCl >60, every 24 h if 30-60, every 36-48 h if 10-30 mL/min). It accumulates and the proarrhythmia risk rises in renal impairment.
hepatic: Sotalol is not metabolised by the liver and is not significantly protein-bound, so no dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment.

major: Other QT-prolonging drugs (class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antiemetics) - additive QT prolongation and torsades risk; avoid
Drugs causing hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia (e.g. potassium-wasting diuretics) - increase torsades risk
Other beta-blockers/non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) - additive bradycardia, AV block, hypotension and negative inotropy
moderate: Digoxin - additive bradycardia/AV block; proarrhythmia more frequent in digoxin-treated patients
Catecholamine-depleting agents (e.g. reserpine, guanethidine) - excessive bradycardia/hypotension
Insulin and oral hypoglycaemics - sotalol may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms and affect glucose control
Clonidine - risk of rebound hypertension if clonidine is withdrawn during beta-blockade
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach; food, milk and especially antacids reduce sotalol absorption (give 2 hours apart from antacids)
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol - additive hypotension and CNS depression
interactions.diagnostics: Prolongs the QT interval on ECG; can mask tachycardia of hypoglycaemia; monitor electrolytes and ECG

serious: Proarrhythmia, including torsades de pointes and worsening ventricular arrhythmia
Marked bradycardia, sinus arrest or high-grade AV block
emergency: Torsades de pointes / syncope from ventricular arrhythmia
Severe symptomatic bradycardia or complete heart block

monitoring: Baseline and on-treatment ECG with QT/QTc measurement (2-4 hours after dosing during initiation/titration)
Heart rate and rhythm; blood pressure
Serum potassium and magnesium (correct before and during therapy)
Renal function/creatinine clearance to guide dose interval
Signs of heart failure, bronchospasm and proarrhythmia (syncope, palpitations)
counsel: This medicine controls dangerous heart rhythms but can occasionally cause new rhythm problems, so it is started in hospital with heart tracing monitoring
Take it on an empty stomach (about 1-2 hours before food) and keep antacids well separated
Do not miss doses or stop suddenly - stopping abruptly can be dangerous for the heart
Report fainting, palpitations, marked dizziness, breathlessness or a very slow pulse immediately
Tell every prescriber you take sotalol; many medicines (including some antibiotics, antifungals and antiemetics) can interact and affect the heart rhythm
Keep up regular blood tests for kidney function and salts (potassium/magnesium)
pk: Beta-blocking effect within 1-2 hours of an oral dose
Plasma peak about 2.5-4 hours; bioavailability near 90-100% (reduced by food)
Elimination half-life approximately 12 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Effects last about 12 hours, supporting twice-daily dosing in normal renal function
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from moisture; oral solution per label
pearls: BOXED WARNING: proarrhythmia (including torsades de pointes); INITIATE/re-initiate/uptitrate in hospital with continuous ECG and QT monitoring, generally for at least 3 days
Dose by creatinine clearance - sotalol is eliminated renally and largely unchanged; risk rises with renal impairment
Do not start if baseline QTc >450 ms; reduce/stop if QTc reaches >=500 ms on treatment
Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia and avoid other QT-prolonging drugs
It is both a non-selective beta-blocker (class II) and a class III agent - take on an empty stomach, do not stop abruptly
No hepatic dose adjustment (not metabolised by the liver); can mask hypoglycaemia and cause bronchospasm
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, but skip it if your next dose is near - never take two doses together, as this can dangerously prolong the QT interval. Do not stop the drug suddenly; contact your doctor if you miss several doses.
overdose: Overdose causes bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, heart failure, hypoglycaemia, marked QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, and in severe cases asystole. Treat supportively: atropine, beta-agonists or temporary pacing for bradycardia, intravenous fluids/inotropes and glucagon for hypotension and beta-blockade, bronchodilators for bronchospasm, and magnesium plus overdrive pacing/isoprenaline for torsades. Sotalol is dialysable, so haemodialysis can reduce plasma levels.
